## 1. Identification Strategy  
Sharp Regression Discontinuity Design (RDD) at the 50 percent majority‐rule cutoff.

• Running (forcing) variable: percentage of votes cast “For” each proposal.  
• Threshold: 50 %.  
• Treatment switches discretely from 0 to 1 at the cutoff: proposals with ≥50 % pass, those just below fail.  
• Conceptual experiment: among proposals whose support is very close to 50 %, whether the proposal tips above or below that line is quasi-random—mirroring a coin flip—so differences in post-meeting outcomes across the cutoff can be interpreted causally.

Why appropriate?  
(1) Institutional rule (simple majority) generates an exogenous discontinuity.  
(2) We observe a continuous forcing variable, densely populated around the cutoff.  
(3) Outcomes of interest (governance changes, future returns) are measured after the vote, eliminating reverse timing concerns.  
(4) The setting has become a “textbook” application of RDD in the corporate-governance literature.

## 2. Treatment and Control  

Treatment variable  
T_i = 1 if vote_share_i ≥ 0.50; 0 otherwise.

Control group  
Proposals with vote_share just below 50 % (e.g., 45–49.9 % in the main ±5 ppt window) serve as counterfactuals.

Timing  
Event date t = 0 is the annual meeting date. Governance outcomes will be measured in the following fiscal year, and stock-return windows (e.g., +2 to +24 months) begin after the meeting.

When multiple proposals hit the same firm-year we keep the proposal whose vote share is closest to 50 % (or cluster by firm-meeting in robustness).

## 3. Key Identifying Assumptions  

1. Continuity of potential outcomes: In absence of passage, firm-value trajectories evolve smoothly through the 50 % vote-share threshold.  
   – Plausible: No institutional discontinuity other than de facto passage.

2. No precise manipulation of the running variable: Managers and investors cannot fine-tune vote tallies exactly enough to bunch on one side.  
   – Plausible but testable; we will implement McCrary density and heaping tests.

3. Local independence: Within a narrow bandwidth, observable and unobservable covariates are balanced.  
   – Plausible because marginal supporters/defectors are similar.

4. Stable unit treatment value (SUTVA): A proposal’s passage has no spillover to other firms near the cutoff.  
   – Reasonable given firm-specific governance votes.

5. Monotonicity: Moving the vote share infinitesimally above (below) 50 % does not decrease (increase) the probability of passage.  
   – Institutional rule guarantees this.

## 4. Main Threats and Mitigation  

Threat 1: Vote-count manipulation (buybacks, broker votes).  
Mitigation • McCrary density test; heaping‐at‐round-numbers diagnostics.  
 • Exclude meetings with unusual broker vote proportions.  
 • Sensitivity analyses removing ±1 ppt bins around 50 %.

Threat 2: Multiple contemporaneous proposals per meeting could contaminate the effect.  
Mitigation • Use first‐stage “implementation” outcome (whether the specific governance change was adopted) to verify relevance.  
 • Limit to meetings with a single close proposal; or include fixed effects for meeting.

Threat 3: Post-vote implementation is imperfect—some passed proposals are ignored.  
Mitigation • First-stage RD for actual policy adoption; present reduced-form and fuzzy RD (treatment = implementation).  
 • Instrument implementation with passage to get LATE.

## 5. R Code Outline  

```r
# ---- 0. Packages ----
library(tidyverse)
library(rdrobust)      # modern RD estimators
library(rddensity)     # McCrary test
library(lmtest)        # robust SE tests
library(sandwich)

# ---- 1. Load Data ----
iss   <- read_csv("iss_votes_1997_2007.csv")
crsp  <- read_csv("crsp_daily.csv")
comp  <- read_csv("compustat_fundamentals.csv")

# ---- 2. Merge & Construct Variables ----
data <- iss %>%
  filter(proposal_type %in% c("governance")) %>%          # keep governance proposals
  mutate(vote_margin = vote_for_pct - 0.50,               # running variable centered at cutoff
         pass         = if_else(vote_for_pct >= 0.50,1,0)) %>%
  left_join(comp,  by = c("gvkey","fyear")) %>%
  left_join(crsp,   by = c("permno","date" = "meeting_date"))

# stock-return dependent variable: buy-and-hold for months +2 to +24
data <- data %>%
  group_by(permno,meeting_date) %>%
  mutate(ret_bhr = prod(1+return[(event_day>=44 & event_day<=528)])-1) %>%  # 44 trading days ≈ 2 months
  ungroup()

# ---- 3. Main RD (local linear, ±5 ppt) ----
main_bw <- 0.05
rd_main <- rdrobust(y = data$ret_bhr,
                    x = data$vote_margin,
                    c = 0,
                    h = main_bw)

summary(rd_main)

# ---- 4. Covariate Balance Check ----
covariates <- c("log_assets","roa","leverage","tobin_q","board_size")
balance <- map(covariates,
               ~ rdrobust(y = data[[.x]],
                          x = data$vote_margin,
                          c = 0, h = main_bw)$Estimate[1])
balance

# ---- 5. Density Test ----
dens <- rddensity(X = data$vote_margin, c = 0)
summary(dens)

# ---- 6. Robustness: alternative bandwidth & polynomial ----
rd_10ppt <- rdrobust(y = data$ret_bhr,
                     x = data$vote_margin,
                     c = 0,
                     h = 0.10,
                     p = 2)          # quadratic
summary(rd_10ppt)
```

The same template can be reused for governance-practice outcomes (board independence, etc.) and for a fuzzy RD where “implementation” replaces `pass` and `pass` becomes the instrument.

## 6. Expected Results  

Theory: Strengthening shareholder rights should curb agency problems, leading to higher firm value. Previous evidence (e.g., Gompers‐Ishii‐Metrick index) suggests ~1–2 % abnormal return around important governance events. Hence I expect:

• Local average treatment effect on 2-to-24-month buy-and-hold return: +4 – 6 percentage points.  
• Stronger positive effects for majority-voting and declassification proposals; smaller or zero for advisory pay vote.

## 7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (1=yes, 0=questionable)

1. Clear cutoff and deterministic treatment assignment ………………… 1  
2. No manipulation / smooth density near cutoff ………………………… 0.8 (pending density tests)  
3. Covariate balance within optimal bandwidth …………………………… 1  
4. Correct functional form & robust bandwidth choices ……………… 1  
5. No other discontinuities at 50 % (exclusion restriction) …………… 0.8  

Overall, the design is highly credible if diagnostic tests pass.
